messages:
sanjay: Quick thought — our current fixed-window continuous batcher (50ms window) is simple but I keep seeing p95 spikes for small high-priority requests. Thinking about an adaptive-window that shrinks when queue depth is low and expands when busy. Anyone tried this pattern at scale?
laura: yeah we prototyped something similar last year. main win is lower median latency for low QPS routes, but tail can get weird if you let window oscillate. need dampening. :thinking_face:
noah: the other failure mode is starvation: tiny requests never hit batch size and get stuck if adaptive logic biases toward larger windows. age-release (force-send after X ms per item) helps.
riley: +1 for age-release. also consider token-aware batching — requests with longer generation budgets should not block short token requests. we used per-request token_estimate in the drain policy.
amanda: we must keep SLO isolation in mind. For enterprise customers we promised p95 <= 300ms for interactive routes. Adaptive windowing can help average but might break p95 unless combined with priority lanes or reserved capacity.
ci-bot: experiment started: experiments/awindow-v1 on eng-runtime canary pool (config: base_window=50ms, min=10ms, max=200ms, alpha=0.4)
sanjay: good point about lanes. rough idea: keep 2 logical lanes — interactive and bulk. adaptive window applies only to interactive lane. bulk still uses larger fixed window for throughput. thoughts?
laura: that seems sensible. interactive lane: adaptive window + age-release + token caps. bulk lane: batch until either size or timeout. keep routing policy deterministic so metrics map to routes.
noah: pseudocode I sketched earlier, pasted here for clarity:
```
function drain_loop():
  while true:
    qd = queue.depth()
    window = clamp(base_window * (1 - alpha * (1 - min(qd / target_depth, 1))), min_window, max_window)
    items = queue.collect_until(window, max_items)
    for item in items:
      if now - item.enqueue_time > max_age: send(item)
    send_batch(items)
```
notes: max_age ensures no starvation; token-aware collect_until stops adding if token_estimate_sum > token_budget.
riley: nice. couple of operational checks:
- ensure deterministic batch ids for debugging
- expose window and queue_fill metrics per shard
- early-fallback: if batch formation exceeds latency SLO, fallback to smaller model or lower-quality quant profile (depends on route)
amanda: fallback sounds risky but aligns with our graceful degradation story. also add a safety valve: if tail latency > threshold, temporarily pin interactive lane to a dedicated small pool.
sanjay: simulation plan: run closed-loop sim with realistic arrival traces (burstiness + skew across routes), evaluate p50/p95/p99, token cost, and fairness (per-route slowdown). assign canary to 10% traffic after sim if results look okay.
laura: also instrument per-request metadata: requested_model, token_estimate, route_priority. we can then slice metrics by those dims.
noah: one more: admission control vs adaptive window. If capacity constrained, admission should reject or queue with backpressure header so downstream can adapt. Adaptive window doesn't remove need for admission.
ci-bot: reminder: perf regression job queued: perf/awindow-v1-e2e (ETA 2h)
sanjay: action items: 1) laura to add age-release + token-aware drain to prototype (this week) 2) noah to build simulator with burst traces 3) riley to define per-route qos knobs + observability dashboard 4) amanda to draft fallback/pinning playbook. will reconvene after perf job. :thumbsup:
laura: ack, starting prototype PR now.
noah: I'll seed simulator with last 3 months traffic traces, will share dashboard.
riley: drafting QoS config schema — will post short RFC.
amanda: will write runbook snippets for pinning and fallback policies.
sanjay: thanks all. if perf/awindow-v1-e2e looks good we can canary next week.
ci-bot: perf run completed: perf/awindow-v1-e2e -> succeeded (results: p50 -6ms, p95 -20ms for interactive lane; detailed report in #perf-results)
